questions.explanation: Constness of a `span` is shallow, like a pointer: `const std::span<int>` is a constant view, but the elements are still `int`, so `operator[]` returns `int&`. To forbid writes you need `std::span<const int>`. The program therefore compiles and prints `42`.

A `std::span<int>` can only be built from a range whose elements are convertible without dropping `const`, and `cr` gives `const int`. Line (1) adds `const`, which is allowed, (3) is an exact match, and (4) is an array of the right static size, which converts implicitly.

The default layout is `std::layout_right`, which is row-major: the last index varies fastest, so element `[1, 2]` of a 3 by 4 view lives at offset `1 * 4 + 2 = 6`. The value `7` is what `layout_left`, the column-major layout, would give for `1 + 2 * 3`.

questions.explanation: A `span` can be built from an rvalue range only when its element type is `const` (or the range is a borrowed range), because then the usual hazard is considered acceptable, so the declaration compiles. The span stores only a pointer and a size, so no lifetime extension applies, and the vector is destroyed at the end of the declaration. The loop then reads freed memory. With `std::span<int>` the declaration would be ill-formed.

questions.explanation: `subspan(offset, count)` requires `offset <= size()` and, when `count` is given, `count <= size() - offset`. Here `offset == 1` leaves 2 elements, so asking for 3 breaks the precondition. Calls (1) and (2) take the full size and zero, and (3) uses `offset == size()`, which is valid and gives an empty span, so it is not the off-by-one trap it looks like.

questions.explanation: The template overloads `first<Count>`, `last<Count>` and `subspan<Offset, Count>` always return a span with a static extent, even when the source has a dynamic one. They carry a precondition `Count <= size()`, which is not checked by the type system. The function-argument overloads such as `first(2)` return a dynamic-extent span.
